citations.quote:
Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

Let $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Put $M:=\sum_{i}m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$; all sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$ (the index set $\{1,\dots,N\}$ of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

derivations.claim: The interval $J$ has nonempty interior, hence at least two points, and each $x_{i}$ is differentiable on $J$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); so the hypotheses of [L2] are met with $I:=J$. Its first clause gives differentiability of $X$ and each $\rho_{i}$, the formula $X'=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}'$, the formula $\rho_{i}'=x_{i}'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$ and $\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}'=0$ on $J$.
Writing $x_{i}'=w_{i}$ by [L1], the formula of step 1.1 reads $X'=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}w_{i}=M^{-1}P$, so $P=MV$ and $X'=M^{-1}P$; together with step 1.1 this is clause 1.

Clause 2: multiply the splitting identity of [L2] by $\frac12$ and substitute $x_{i}'=w_{i}$ and $X'=V$; the left side is $K$ by [L1], and the two right-hand terms are $\frac12M\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}$ and $\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert\rho_{i}'\rVert_{2}^{2}$.

Clause 3: for $N=2$, the two-body clause of [L2] gives $\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert\rho_{i}'\rVert_{2}^{2}=\mu\lVert r'\rVert_{2}^{2}$ with $r=x_{1}-x_{2}$ and $\mu=m_{1}m_{2}/M$; substituting into step 3.1 gives the displayed two-body splitting.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes the centre-of-mass mass-weighted decomposition on the model label set with N>=1. Consequently the displayed particle sums have a nonempty finite index set; N=0 is excluded by the model hypotheses, rather than silently assigned a centre of mass or total mass.
Zero data are included: a zero velocity field makes K=0 and every clause reads 0=0; the proof steps 1.1-4.1 are identities and divide by no quantity.
N=1 is included: the sums reduce to one term and clauses 1-2 still hold (statement); clause 3 is asserted only for N=2.
The only degenerate parameter is M=0, excluded by m_i>0 in the statement; no other degeneracy enters the algebraic identities of steps 1.1-4.1.
The interval J need not be open; differentiability is asserted at every point of J and clause 3 holds at every t in J, with no one-sided endpoint limit used (statement).

boundaries.reason: No selection from a family is made; the argument only rearranges the given finite sums.
No equivalence is asserted; the clauses are identities and a two-body substitution.
The Statement derives centre-of-mass, relative-velocity and kinetic-energy identities for the declared positive masses; it does not claim those identities characterize a force model.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–4.1 and the full mathematical splitting supplier checked. Positive masses and N>=1 ensure M>0; C2 curves satisfy differentiability on the nondegenerate interval including relative endpoint derivatives. Weighted relative velocities sum to zero, removing the cross term. For N=2 the coefficient is m1*m2/M; N=1 relative term is zero. No dynamics or conservation used. Tong Eq.1.15,1.22–1.23, PDF pp.12,14 checked. Finite coordinate sums use no AC. Likharev Eqs3.30–3.35 retrieved at chapter3 p8/PDF40; repaired the inaccurate printed-page locator, with no formula change.

citations.quote:
Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $N\ge1$, let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$, and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice differentiable, i.e. differentiable with derivative $x_i'$ differentiable ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $p_i:=m_ix_i'$ and suppose there are maps $f_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ and, for every ordered pair $i\ne j$ in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, maps $f_{ij}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ such that

$$f_{ij}(t)=-f_{ji}(t),\qquad p_i'(t)=f_i(t)+\sum_{j\ne i}f_{ij}(t)\qquad(t\in I).$$

Write $P:=\sum_ip_i$, $J:=\sum_ix_i\times p_i$ (cross product in $\mathbb R^3$, [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then:

1. $P$ is differentiable on $I$ with $P'(t)=\sum_if_i(t)$ for all $t\in I$;
2. $J$ is differentiable on $I$ with $$J'(t)=\sum_ix_i(t)\times f_i(t)+\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_i(t)-x_j(t)\bigr)\times f_{ij}(t)\qquad(t\in I);$$
3. if in addition, for every $i<j$, $f_{ij}$ is parallel to $x_i-x_j$ — that is, there is a real function $\lambda_{ij}$ on $I$ with $f_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}(x_i-x_j)$ — then $J'(t)=\sum_ix_i(t)\times f_i(t)$ for all $t\in I$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

derivations.claim: Define, for $t\in J$, $$f_{i}(t):=F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad f_{ij}(t):=F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr)\quad(i\ne j).$$ These are well-defined functions $J\to\mathbb R^{3}$: the evaluated arguments lie in the stated domains of the pair presentation and of the model's state domain, and the presentation is an identity for $F_{i}$ there. By the antisymmetry clause, $f_{ij}(t)=-f_{ji}(t)$ for all $i\ne j$ and $t\in J$.

Each $p_{i}=m_{i}w_{i}$ is differentiable on $J$ with $p_{i}'=m_{i}\ddot x_{i}$; by the equation of motion and the presentation this equals $$F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)=f_{i}(t)+\sum_{j\ne i}f_{ij}(t)\qquad(t\in J).$$ Thus the data of [L2] are met on the interval $J$ with the maps $f_{i}$, $f_{ij}$ of step 1.1, and [L2] yields that $P$ is differentiable on $J$ with $$P'(t)=\sum_{i}f_{i}(t)=\sigma(t);$$ $P'$ is continuous because the $f_{i}$ are continuous, so $P$ is $C^{1}$ on $J$, and clause 1 is proved.

Clause 2: if $\sigma\equiv0$ on $J$, then $P'=0$ at every interior point of $J$ by step 2.1, and $P$ is continuous on $J$; [L3] gives that $P$ is constant on $J$; then $V=M^{-1}P$ is constant on $J$ as a constant multiple.

Clause 3: by clause 1 of [[pthm-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-kinetic-splitting]] applied to the motion (which is a $C^{2}$ curve family), $X$ is differentiable on $J$ with $X'=M^{-1}P$; since $P$ is $C^{1}$ by step 2.1, $X'$ is $C^{1}$, so $X$ is $C^{2}$ with $$X''=M^{-1}P'=M^{-1}\sigma,$$ that is $MX''=\sigma$, which is clause 3.

boundaries.evidence: For N=1 the internal pair sums are empty and the balance reduces to P'=sigma; the reindexing argument of step 2.1 handles the empty case vacuously.
The hypothesis sigma identically zero of clause 2 is exactly the zero case, treated in step 4.1 (constant P).
N=1 is included: there are no pair forces and clause 1 reads P'=F_1^ext; step 2.1 applies with an empty internal sum.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate parameter occurs; the proof divides by no quantity (masses enter only through p_i=m_i x_i').

boundaries.evidence: Conservation is concluded on the whole interval J in step 4.1 from a vanishing interior derivative and continuity of P; no endpoint derivative is taken.

boundaries.reason: No selection from a family is made; the argument reindexes finite sums only.
Clause 2 is one-directional (vanishing total external force implies constant P); no equivalence is asserted.
The converse is not asserted, so no reverse direction is claimed or proved.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–4.1 and full mathematical momentum supplier checked: evaluation on shared pair domains preserves antisymmetry; finite pair cancellation gives P prime=sigma with sigma continuous. Zero derivative applied coordinatewise gives constancy including endpoints; X prime=P/M yields MX double prime=sigma. Positive M, N=1 empty pair sum and vanishing forces checked. Refuter 19:1 confirmed: two free labels, subsystem {1}, no external forces yields constant momentum with no exchange. Repaired the remark to possible exchange, with explicit zero-total-external-force conservation. Formal claims unchanged. Tong §1.3, PDF p12 and Fitzpatrick Eq.41 checked. No empirical premise or AC.

citations.quote:
Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Internal torque identity. Using [L4] and the antisymmetry of the pair maps, $$\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}-o\bigr)\times\sum_{j\ne i}F_{ij}=\sum_{i<j}\Bigl[\bigl(x_{i}-o\bigr)\times F_{ij}+\bigl(x_{j}-o\bigr)\times F_{ji}\Bigr]=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}-x_{j}\bigr)\times F_{ij}=I,$$ because $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ and the cross product is bilinear by [L3]; the first equality also shows $I$ does not depend on $o$. Adding $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}=\sum_{i}(x_{i}-o)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and substituting the presentation $F_{i}=F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}+\sum_{j\ne i}F_{ij}$ gives $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$, completing clause 1.

Balance. Each summand $(x_{i}-o)\times p_{i}$ of $J_{o}$ is a cross product of curves differentiable on $J$ (since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$ and $o$ is $C^{1}$), so by [L2] $J_{o}$ is differentiable on $J$ with $$J_{o}'=\sum_{i}\bigl(w_{i}-o'\bigr)\times p_{i}+\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}-o\bigr)\times p_{i}'.$$ In the first sum, $\sum_{i}w_{i}\times p_{i}=\sum_{i}m_{i}\,w_{i}\times w_{i}=0$ by alternation [L3], so it equals $-o'\times P$; in the second sum, substitute $p_{i}'=m_{i}\ddot x_{i}=F_{i}(t,x,w)$ from the equation of motion, which gives $\sum_{i}(x_{i}-o)\times F_{i}=T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ by clause 1. Therefore $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I-o'\times P$, which is clause 2.

Centrality. Under the hypothesis of clause 3, for each $i<j$ $$\bigl(x_{i}-x_{j}\bigr)\times F_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}\,\bigl(x_{i}-x_{j}\bigr)\times\bigl(x_{i}-x_{j}\bigr)=0$$ by alternation and bilinearity [L3]; hence $I=0$ and step 2.1 gives $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}-o'\times P$. If $o$ is constant then $o'=0$ and $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$.

Conservation. Let $o$ be constant and $T_{o}\equiv0$ on $J$. Then $o'=0$ and step 2.1 gives $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I=T_{o}=0$ at every interior point of $J$. $J_{o}$ is continuous on $J$, being a finite sum of products of continuous curves; [L5] gives that $J_{o}$ is constant on $J$. In the particular case, step 3.1 gives $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ when the evaluated pair forces are central and the external torque vanishes; this includes a model with no external forces.

boundaries.evidence: For N=1 the internal torque sum I is empty, hence zero, and clause 2 reduces to J_o'=T_o^ext-o' times P; step 1.1 and step 3.1 treat the empty reindexing vacuously.

The zero and constant reference curves are included: step 2.1 allows any C^1 curve o and step 4.1 takes o'=0; the zero total torque T_o identically zero is the hypothesis of clause 4, discharged in step 4.1.
N=1 is included: the internal torque sum is empty and hence zero, so clause 2 of the statement reads J_o'=T_o^ext-o' times P; the reindexing argument of step 1.1 applies vacuously.
Coincident positions x_i=x_j are not needed: centrality is assumed only for the evaluated pairs in clause 3, and step 4.1 computes (x_i-x_j) times F_ij directly without dividing by a separation.
J_o is differentiable on J and continuous on J, and clause 4 concludes constancy on J in step 4.1 via the zero-derivative corollary; no endpoint derivative is used.

boundaries.reason: No selection from a family is made and no choice principle is invoked; all reindexings are finite.
No equivalence is asserted; the centrality clause is a sufficient condition and the conservation clause is one-directional.
No converse of the centrality clause is claimed in the theorem (the companion counterexample addresses that question separately).

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–4.1 checked: disjoint ordered pairs regroup to (x_i-x_j) cross F_ij by antisymmetry; differentiation cancels w_i cross m_i w_i and retains -o prime cross P. Centrality is sufficient even at coincidence when the stated scalar-multiple condition holds; total zero torque suffices independently. Apply zero-derivative theorem componentwise, including endpoints by continuity. N=1 gives an empty pair sum. Exact pairing, reindexing and cross-product supplier statements checked. Tong §§1.2–1.3, PDF pp.9–14, and Fitzpatrick Eqs.38–44 checked; Tong’s wording of necessity is not adopted. No empirical or choice premise.

citations.quote:
Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
