citations.quote:
Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Adopt, whenever a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]
invokes them, the following **restricted interaction assumptions**. Throughout,
the data $I_{0}$, $Q$, $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$ and the force map $F$ are those of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], and a state writes $z=(x,v)$ with
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})\in Q$ and $v=(v_{1},\dots,v_{N})\in\mathbb R^{3N}$.

**(i) External-plus-pair decomposition.** The model's force map is presented as

$$F_{i}(t,z)=F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_{i},v_{i})+\sum_{j\ne i}F_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j},v_{i},v_{j}) \qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

where each $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a single-label **external** force map and
each $F_{ij}$ (for $i\ne j$, an ordered pair) is a **pair** force map, all
defined on their stated open domains and satisfying the standing continuity
and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause (iii) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with respect to the arguments they actually
depend on. This is a restriction of the model class: an arbitrary force map
$F$ of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] need not admit such a decomposition,
and the decomposition is part of the model's declaration, not a theorem. It is
relative to the declared set of labels: for a subsystem, a pair force to a
label outside the declared set appears as an external force, and no
antisymmetry or pairing property of the full system restricts that external
force.

**(ii) Optional pair assumptions.** In addition, a model may adopt, separately
or together, the following assumptions about a pair force $F_{ij}$:

1. **Antisymmetry (strong form of the third law).**
   $F_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j},v_{i},v_{j})=-F_{ji}(t,x_{j},x_{i},v_{j},v_{i})$ for
   all arguments in the domain.
2. **Centrality.** $F_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j},v_{i},v_{j})$ is parallel to
   $x_{i}-x_{j}$, i.e. lies in the real line spanned by $x_{i}-x_{j}$,
   whenever $x_{i}\ne x_{j}$.

Each assumption is a further restriction of the model class and is adopted
only where invoked. Both are *sufficient* hypotheses used by later balance
statements, and neither is a consequence of the equation of motion: a
velocity-dependent pair force, or an interaction mediated by a field omitted
from the declared labels, need satisfy neither.

**(iii) Potential model.** A model may present its force map through a scalar
**potential** $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules ([[def-cm01-units]]), through the rule

$$F_{i}(t,z)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

the gradient being the Euclidean gradient in the position variable of each
label ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). This is a restriction of the force class:
only force maps that are the negative gradient of such a potential belong to
it. The same force map arises from every potential of the form
$U(t,x)+c(t)$ with a differentiable function $c$ of $t$ alone whenever
the declared $C^{2}$ regularity is retained. More generally, for each connected
component $C$ of $Q$ (a maximal connected subset), two $C^{2}$ potentials
for the same force differ by an independently chosen $C^{2}$ function
$c_C(t)$ on $I_0\times C$. A single time function suffices when $Q$ is
connected; openness alone does not require the constants on different
components to agree. The chosen normalization is part of any later energy
statement and is recorded with it, and no energy statement is made on this page.

**(iv) Pair and external potentials are examples, not the general form.**
When $U$ has the form

$$U(t,x)=\sum_{i}u_{i}(t,x_{i})+\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j})$$

with $C^{2}$ scalar functions $u_{i}$, $u_{ij}$, the decomposition (i) holds
with $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}=-\nabla_{x_{i}}u_{i}$ and
$F_{ij}=-\nabla_{x_{i}}u_{ij}$. Potentials of the still more special form
$u_{ij}=u_{ij}(t,\lvert x_{i}-x_{j}\rvert)$ are the **central pair
potentials**; these are examples, and no generality is claimed for any of
these subclasses. Velocity-dependent forces such as the drag model
[[post-cm02-drag]] lie outside every potential model of this clause.

**(v) Newtonian gravitational branch.** The model may adopt the pair potential

$$U_{ij}(x_{i},x_{j})=-\frac{G_{\mathrm N}\,m_{i}^{g}m_{j}^{g}}{\lvert x_{i}-x_{j}\rvert}$$

on the collision-excluded configuration domain ($x_{i}\ne x_{j}$ for all
$i\ne j$), where $G_{\mathrm N}>0$ is a constant of dimension
$\ell^{3}\mu^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]) and the numbers
$m_{1}^{g},\dots,m_{N}^{g}>0$ are **gravitational coupling parameters** of the
labels, primitive model data distinct from the inertial masses $m_{i}$ of the
equation of motion. By clause (iii) this potential supplies the attractive
inverse-square pair force
$F_{ij}=-G_{\mathrm N}m_{i}^{g}m_{j}^{g}\,(x_{i}-x_{j})/\lvert x_{i}-x_{j}\rvert^{3}$,
the content of the elementary differentiation
$\nabla_{x}\bigl(1/\lvert x-y\rvert\bigr)=-(x-y)/\lvert x-y\rvert^{3}$; a
concrete instance of that differentiation is verified on the companion page.
The adopted model satisfies the antisymmetry and centrality options of (ii)
where they are invoked.

**(vi) The mass identification is an empirical assumption.** The
identification

$$m_{i}^{g}=m_{i}\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

of gravitational couplings with inertial masses is **not** part of clauses
(i)–(v) and is not a consequence of the equation of motion. It is an
additional empirical assumption, adopted only when a model states it, and it
is the subject of the weak equivalence principle; the sources record its
empirical support and its historical status, and this page records no
measurement. Likewise, the inverse-square form in (v) is an adopted law, not a
consequence of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]].

**(vii) Status.** Clauses (i)–(v) are adopted modelling assumptions that
restrict the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; they add no
dynamics beyond that postulate, and every theorem of this page remains
conditional on these adopted hypotheses. The balances of momentum, angular
momentum and energy, when asserted later, are theorems with their own
hypotheses on this structure and are not made here.

Adopt the force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: time window
$I_{0}$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, and a force map $F$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in
the state variable, locally uniformly in time, on
$D=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Let
$\mathcal F(t,x,v)=\bigl(v,\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\bigr)$ be the associated
first-order field and let motions and maximal motions be as in
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Fix an initial datum
$(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})\in I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and write
$z_{0}=(x_{0},v_{0})$.

1. **Local existence.** There is $h>0$ and there is a motion $x$ of the model
   on $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$;
   moreover such a motion is exactly one of class $C^{2}$ satisfying
   $m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}(t,x(t),\dot x(t))$ for all $i$ and all
   $t\in[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$.
2. **Uniqueness.** If $x:J\to Q$ and $\tilde x:\tilde J\to Q$ are motions of
   the model with the same initial datum,
   $x(t_{0})=\tilde x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and $\dot x(t_{0})=\dot{\tilde x}(t_{0})=v_{0}$,
   then $x=\tilde x$ on $J\cap\tilde J$.
3. **Quantitative cylinder.** Let $h,r>0$ satisfy
   $C:=[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]\times\overline B(z_{0},r)\subseteq D$, put
   $M:=\sup\{\lVert\mathcal F(t,z)\rVert_{2}:(t,z)\in C\}$ and let $\Lambda$
   be a state-Lipschitz constant of $\mathcal F$ on $C$. If $hM\le r$ and
   $\Lambda h<1$, then there is exactly one motion on $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$
   through the datum whose state graph $(t,(x(t),\dot x(t)))$ lies in $C$, and
   every motion through the datum agrees with it on the intersection of its
   interval with $[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$.
4. **Maximal motion.** There is exactly one maximal motion with the datum:
   its maximal interval $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing $t_{0}$ and
   contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the datum is its restriction.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force model: clause 1 locates a
solution only near $t_{0}$ and bounds no interval length in terms of the data,
clause 4 asserts no completeness of $J_{\max}$ in $I_{0}$, and no empirical
content is claimed.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], and suppose in addition that the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]],
$$F_{i}(t,z)=F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_{i},v_{i})+\sum_{j\ne i}F_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j},v_{i},v_{j}),$$
with the antisymmetry clause (ii)1 of that postulate,
$F_{ij}(t,x_{i},x_{j},v_{i},v_{j})=-F_{ji}(t,x_{j},x_{i},v_{j},v_{i})$ on the
common domain. Let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion of the model on an interval $J$ with
nonempty interior, with quantities $M$, $P$, $X$, $V$ as in the definition,
and write
$$\sigma(t):=\sum_{i}F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J)$$
for the **total external force along the motion**. Then:

1. $P$ is of class $C^{1}$ on $J$ and
   $$\dot P(t)=\sigma(t)\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the total momentum changes at the rate of the total external force, the
   internal pair forces cancelling in the sum;
2. if $\sigma\equiv0$ on $J$, then $P$ is constant on $J$ and $V=M^{-1}P$ is
   constant on $J$;
3. $X$ is of class $C^{2}$ on $J$ and
   $$M\,X''(t)=\sigma(t)\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the centre of mass obeys the equation of a single particle of mass $M$
   under the total external force.

The statement assumes the pair presentation and its antisymmetry; for a model
whose force map is not presented through such pairs it asserts nothing, and
the pair forces of the presentation need not be central (centrality is used
only in the angular-momentum balance of this page). No empirical content is
claimed.

Adopt the force model, the inertial frame and the notation of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, a
curve family $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ on an interval $J$ with nonempty
interior, coordinate velocities $w_{i}=x_{i}'$, and the quantities
$$M=\sum_{i}m_{i},\qquad P=\sum_{i}m_{i}w_{i},\qquad X=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i},\qquad \rho_{i}=x_{i}-X,\qquad V=X',\qquad K=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}.$$
Then:

1. $P=MV$ on $J$, that is $X'=M^{-1}P$, and the identities
   $$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0,\qquad \sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}'=0$$
   hold on $J$;
2. for every $t\in J$,
   $$K(t)=\frac12M\lVert V(t)\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert\rho_{i}'(t)\rVert_{2}^{2};$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_{1}-x_{2}$ and $\mu:=m_{1}m_{2}/M$ one has, for
   every $t\in J$,
   $$K(t)=\frac12M\lVert V(t)\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_{2}^{2}.$$

The statement is an identity for the stated curves and masses in the fixed
frame; it uses no equation of motion, no property of the force map and no
conservation claim. The values are frame-dependent; the transformation laws
are the frame-transformation item of this page.

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], and suppose that the model invokes
the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]
with the antisymmetry clause (ii)1 (as in the momentum balance of this page).
Let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion on an interval $J$ with nonempty interior and let
$o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be a $C^{1}$ reference curve, with $J_{o}$,
$T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ and $P$ as in the definition. Then:

1. **Internal torque identity.** For every $t\in J$,
   $$\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times\sum_{j\ne i}F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr)=I(t),\qquad\text{so}\qquad T_{o}(t)=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t)+I(t);$$
2. **Balance.** $J_{o}$ is differentiable on $J$ and
   $$J_{o}'(t)=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t)+I(t)-o'(t)\times P(t)=T_{o}(t)-o'(t)\times P(t)\qquad(t\in J);$$
3. **Centrality.** Suppose that for every $i<j$ and every $t\in J$ the
   evaluated pair force is parallel to $x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)$, that is, there is
   a real $\lambda_{ij}(t)$ with
   $$F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr)=\lambda_{ij}(t)\,\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
   Then $I\equiv0$ on $J$, so
   $$J_{o}'(t)=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t)-o'(t)\times P(t)\qquad(t\in J);$$
   if moreover $o$ is constant, then $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$;
4. **Conservation.** If $o$ is constant and $T_{o}\equiv0$ on $J$ —
   equivalently $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv-I$ there, by clause 1 — then
   $J_{o}$ is constant on $J$. In particular, if the evaluated pair forces
   are central (clause 3) and $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$ on $J$ — the case
   of a model with no external forces — then $T_{o}\equiv0$ and $J_{o}$ is
   constant on $J$.

Clause 3 allows cancellation: the vanishing of $I$ is a hypothesis on the
evaluated pair forces and does not require centrality in general; the
companion page exhibits antisymmetric non-central pair forces whose internal
torque sum vanishes identically. No empirical content is claimed.

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]: masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, an
open configuration domain $Q$, the force map $F$ with the standing hypotheses
of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii), and the quantities $w_{i}$,
$$K=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}(t,x,w),\,w_{i}\bigr\rangle,\qquad W([t_{0},t_{1}])=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt$$
along a curve family. Let $x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an
interval $J$ with nonempty interior. Then:

1. $K$ is of class $C^{1}$ on $J$ and
   $$K'(t)=\mathcal P(t)\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the rate of change of the kinetic energy equals the power of the total
   force;
2. for all $t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$,
   $$K(t_{1})-K(t_{0})=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt=W([t_{0},t_{1}]):$$
   the change of the kinetic energy equals the work of the total force.

No potential, no pair decomposition and no conservation hypothesis is used:
the identity is a consequence of the equation of motion alone, in the fixed
frame. The power and the work are frame-dependent (see clause 4
of the frame-transformation item of this page); the mechanical energy
statement of the potential branch is the energy balance of this page.

Adopt the force model, one inertial frame, and the potential presentation of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (a): a $C^{2}$ potential
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d_{i}$ of the standing
regularity, with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
on the state domain. Let $x:J\to Q$ be a **motion** of the model on an
interval $J$ with nonempty interior, write $\mathfrak d_{i}(t):=d_{i}(t,x(t),w(t))$
for the evaluated residual forces and
$$E(t):=K(t)+U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)$$
for the mechanical energy of the definition (clause (b)). Then:

1. $E$ is differentiable on $J$ and
   $$E'(t)=\partial_{t}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+\sum_{i}\bigl\langle\mathfrak d_{i}(t),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the mechanical energy changes at the rate of the explicit time dependence
   of the potential plus the power of the residual forces;
2. if $\partial_{t}U\equiv0$ on $I_{0}\times Q$ and each evaluated residual
   force $\mathfrak d_{i}$ vanishes identically along this motion, then $E$ is
   constant on $J$. If, more strongly, every residual-force map $d_i$ vanishes
   on its entire state domain, the model is a global potential model with the
   declared representative $U$;
3. for all $t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$,
   $$K(t_{1})-K(t_{0})=U\bigl(t_{0},x(t_{0})\bigr)-U\bigl(t_{1},x(t_{1})\bigr)+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\Bigl[\partial_{t}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+\sum_{i}\bigl\langle\mathfrak d_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle\Bigr]dt,$$
   equivalently $W([t_{0},t_{1}])=U(t_{0},x(t_{0}))-U(t_{1},x(t_{1}))+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\bigl[\partial_{t}U+\sum_{i}\langle\mathfrak d_{i},w_{i}\rangle\bigr]dt$:
   the work of the total force is the decrease of the potential energy plus
   the work of the explicit time dependence and of the residual forces.

The representative $U$ is the one declared by the model; replacing $U$ by
$U+c(t)$ changes $E$ by $c(t)$ and $E'$ by $c'(t)$, as recorded in
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c). The statement is read
in the fixed frame; no empirical content is claimed.

Adopt the force model and the notation of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], and let
$$F=\bigl(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\bigr),\qquad F'=\bigl(o',u',(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$$
be two inertial frames with coordinates $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$ related by
$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+v\,t+a_{0},\qquad b\in\mathbb R,\ a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3},\ R\in SO(3)$$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1,
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). Let $x:J\to Q$ be a curve family of the
model in the first frame and let
$$\eta_{i}(t'):=R\,x_{i}(t'-b)+v\,(t'-b)+a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b)$$
be the description of the same worldlines in the second frame. Write
$\sigma_{i}(t):=F_{i}(t,x(t),w(t))$ and
$\Sigma(t):=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}(t)$ for the evaluated total forces in the first
frame, and read the second frame's quantities from the description $\eta$
with the transferred force map $F_{*}$ of clause (vi) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $\tilde\sigma_{i}(t'):=F_{*i}(t',\eta(t'),\eta'(t'))$,
$\tilde P:=\sum_{i}m_{i}\eta_{i}'$,
$\tilde X:=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}\eta_{i}$,
$\tilde K:=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert\eta_{i}'\rVert_{2}^{2}$,
$\tilde J_{\tilde o}:=\sum_{i}(\eta_{i}-\tilde o)\times m_{i}\eta_{i}'$ and
$\tilde T_{\tilde o}:=\sum_{i}(\eta_{i}-\tilde o)\times\tilde\sigma_{i}$
for any $C^{1}$ reference curve $\tilde o:J+b\to\mathbb R^{3}$ (clause 3
uses the curve corresponding to $o$),
$\tilde{\mathcal P}:=\sum_{i}\langle\tilde\sigma_{i},\eta_{i}'\rangle$ and
$\tilde W([t_{0}',t_{1}']):=\int_{t_{0}'}^{t_{1}'}\tilde{\mathcal P}(t')\,dt'$
for $t_{0}'\le t_{1}'$ in $J+b$. Then, with all first-frame quantities read
at the corresponding time $t'-b$:

1. **Centre of mass and momentum.**
   $$\tilde X(t')=R\,X(t'-b)+v\,(t'-b)+a_{0},\qquad \tilde X'(t')=R\,V(t'-b)+v,\qquad \tilde P(t')=R\,P(t'-b)+M\,v\,;$$
2. **Kinetic energy.**
   $$\tilde K(t')=K(t'-b)+\bigl\langle v,\,R\,P(t'-b)\bigr\rangle+\frac12M\lVert v\rVert_{2}^{2};$$
3. **Angular momentum and torque.** For every $C^{1}$ reference curve
   $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the definition, let
   $\tilde o(t'):=R\,o(t'-b)+v(t'-b)+a_{0}$ and
   $X_{o}(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}(x_{i}(t)-o(t))=X(t)-o(t)$. Then
   $$\tilde J_{\tilde o}(t')=R\,J_{o}(t'-b)+\bigl(R\,X_{o}(t'-b)\bigr)\times(M\,v),\qquad \tilde T_{\tilde o}(t')=R\,T_{o}(t'-b),$$
   where $T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}(x_{i}(t)-o(t))\times\sigma_{i}(t)$ is the
   evaluated total torque of the first frame about $o(t)$;
4. **Power and work.**
   $$\tilde{\mathcal P}(t')=\mathcal P(t'-b)+\bigl\langle R\,\Sigma(t'-b),\,v\bigr\rangle,$$
   and for every curve family and $t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$
   $$\tilde W\bigl([t_{0}+b,\,t_{1}+b]\bigr)=W([t_{0},t_{1}])+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\bigl\langle R\,\Sigma(t),v\bigr\rangle\,dt.$$
   If in addition $x$ is a motion and the model invokes the pair presentation
   of [[post-cm02-interactions]] with the antisymmetry clause, then
   $\Sigma=P'$ along the motion by [[pthm-cm03-momentum-balance]], and
   $$\tilde W\bigl([t_{0}+b,\,t_{1}+b]\bigr)=W([t_{0},t_{1}])+\bigl\langle R\bigl(P(t_{1})-P(t_{0})\bigr),\,v\bigr\rangle;$$
5. **Potential and mechanical energy.** If the model is a global potential
   model of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (a) with
   potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ and the second
   frame's model declares the **scalar transfer**
   $$U_{*}(t',y):=U\bigl(t'-b,\ R^{\mathsf T}(y_{1}-v(t'-b)-a_{0}),\dots,R^{\mathsf T}(y_{N}-v(t'-b)-a_{0})\bigr),$$
   then $U_{*}$ is $C^{2}$ on its open transferred domain,
   $F_{*i}(t',y,u)=-\nabla_{y_{i}}U_{*}(t',y)$ at corresponding data, and the
   mechanical energies of clause (b) of that definition satisfy
   $$\tilde E(t'):=\tilde K(t')+U_{*}\bigl(t',\eta(t')\bigr)=E(t'-b)+\bigl\langle v,\,R\,P(t'-b)\bigr\rangle+\frac12M\lVert v\rVert_{2}^{2}.$$

Whether the second frame's model uses the scalar transfer of clause 5 is a
modelling declaration; a model whose potential is not transferred by this rule
(for instance a background potential that selects a frame) is a different
model in the second frame, and no transformation law of $E$ is asserted for
it. No empirical content is claimed.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: The curves are $C^{2}$: $e$ is $C^{2}$ by [L3], and $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$ as a sum of the linear curve $t\mapsto Vt$ and a scalar multiple of $e$ [L4]. With $\eta$ of [L3], $$\dot x_{1}=V-\frac R2\omega\eta,\qquad \dot x_{2}=V+\frac R2\omega\eta,\qquad \ddot x_{1}=\frac R2\omega^{2}e,\qquad \ddot x_{2}=-\frac R2\omega^{2}e.$$

Equations of motion. Since $\omega^{2}=2k/m$, on the one hand $m\ddot x_{1}=m\frac R2\omega^{2}e=kRe$; on the other $F_{1}(x_{1},x_{2})=-k(x_{1}-x_{2})=-k(-Re)=kRe$, and these agree. Likewise $m\ddot x_{2}=-kRe=-k(x_{2}-x_{1})=F_{2}$. Hence $x$ is a motion of the model on the whole time window $\mathbb R$, and by [L2] it is the unique maximal motion with its datum.

Total momentum and centre of mass. By step 1.1, $$P=m\dot x_{1}+m\dot x_{2}=2mV,\qquad X=\tfrac12(x_{1}+x_{2})=Vt,\qquad V_{\mathrm{cm}}=X'=V,$$ so $P=2mV$ is constant and equals $MV_{\mathrm{cm}}$; the model has no external forces, consistent with clauses 1 and 2 of [[pthm-cm03-momentum-balance]].

Angular momentum about the origin. By step 1.1, $$p_{1}=mV-m\frac R2\omega\eta,\qquad p_{2}=mV+m\frac R2\omega\eta.$$ Expanding $J_{0}=x_{1}\times p_{1}+x_{2}\times p_{2}$ with $x_{1}=Vt-\frac R2e$ and $x_{2}=Vt+\frac R2e$ by bilinearity [L4], the four types of terms combine as follows: the terms $(Vt)\times mV$ occur twice and gives $2(Vt)\times mV=0$ since $V\times V=0$; the two terms pairing $Vt$ with $\eta$ are equal with opposite signs and cancel; the two terms pairing $e$ with $V$ are equal with opposite signs and cancel; and the two terms pairing $e$ with $\eta$ add: $$J_{0}=2\Bigl(\frac R2\Bigr)^{2}m\omega\,(e\times\eta)=\frac12mR^{2}\omega\,e_{3},$$ where $e\times\eta=e_{3}$ by [L4]. This is constant in $t$.

Kinetic splitting. With $r=x_{1}-x_{2}=-Re$ one has $\dot r=-R\omega\eta$ and $\lVert\dot r\rVert_{2}=R\omega$ by [L3], so the two-body clause of [[pthm-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-kinetic-splitting]] predicts $$K=\frac12M\lVert V_{\mathrm{cm}}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12\mu\lVert\dot r\rVert_{2}^{2}=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12\cdot\frac m2\cdot R^{2}\omega^{2}=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac14mR^{2}\omega^{2}.$$ Directly, with $a:=\frac R2\omega\eta$ and $\lVert a\rVert_{2}=\frac R2\omega$, bilinearity gives $\lVert V-a\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert V+a\rVert_{2}^{2}=2\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\lVert a\rVert_{2}^{2}$, so $$K=\frac12m\bigl(\lVert V-a\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert V+a\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr)=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+m\lVert a\rVert_{2}^{2}=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac14mR^{2}\omega^{2},$$ the same value. The relative positions are $\rho_{1}=-\frac R2e$ and $\rho_{2}=\frac R2e$, so $m\rho_{1}+m\rho_{2}=0$.

Moving origin. For $o(t)=\mathbf Wt$ one has $$J_{o}=\sum_{i}(x_{i}-o)\times p_{i}=J_{0}-o\times P,$$ because $o$ is common to both terms and $\sum_{i}p_{i}=P$; hence, by steps 2.3 and 2.2, $$J_{o}=\frac12mR^{2}\omega\,e_{3}-(\mathbf Wt)\times(2mV)=\frac12mR^{2}\omega\,e_{3}-2mt\,(\mathbf W\times V),$$ so $J_{o}'=-2m(\mathbf W\times V)$. The angular-momentum balance clause 2 of [[pthm-cm03-angular-momentum-balance]] reads $J_{o}'=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I-o'\times P$; here $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ (no external forces) and $I=0$ because the pair force is central ($F_{12}\parallel x_{1}-x_{2}$), while $o'\times P=\mathbf W\times(2mV)=2m(\mathbf W\times V)$, so the balance gives the same value $-2m(\mathbf W\times V)$.

Mechanical energy and power. Here $U(x(t))=\frac12k\lVert r\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac12kR^{2}$ is constant in time, and by step 3.1 and $\omega^{2}=2k/m$, $$E=K+U=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac14mR^{2}\omega^{2}+\frac12kR^{2}=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12kR^{2}+\frac12kR^{2}=m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+kR^{2},$$ constant, as clause 2 of [[pthm-cm03-energy-balance]] predicts (the potential is static and there are no residual forces). For the power identity, using $F_{1}=-kr$, $F_{2}=kr$ and $\dot r=\dot x_{1}-\dot x_{2}$, $$\mathcal P=\langle F_{1},\dot x_{1}\rangle+\langle F_{2},\dot x_{2}\rangle=-k\langle r,\dot x_{1}\rangle+k\langle r,\dot x_{2}\rangle=-k\langle r,\dot r\rangle=-\frac12k\,\frac{d}{dt}\lVert r\rVert_{2}^{2},$$ so the power is the negative derivative of the potential energy; clause 1 of [[pthm-cm03-work-energy]] gives $K'=\mathcal P$, consistent with $E'=0$ and clause 1 of [[pthm-cm03-energy-balance]].

Boost to the centre-of-mass frame. Take the second frame with $b=0$, $a_{0}=0$, $R_{\mathrm{rot}}=I_{3}$ and $v_{\mathrm{boost}}=-V$; the description of the curves is $\eta_{i}(t)=x_{i}(t)-Vt=\mp\frac R2e(t)$, so $\tilde P=m\dot\eta_{1}+m\dot\eta_{2}=0$ and, by [L3], $$\tilde K=\frac12m\Bigl\lVert-\frac R2\omega\eta\Bigr\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12m\Bigl\lVert\frac R2\omega\eta\Bigr\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac14mR^{2}\omega^{2}=\frac12kR^{2}.$$ The frame law of clause 2 of [[pthm-cm03-frame-transformations]] gives $$\tilde K=K+\langle v_{\mathrm{boost}},P\rangle+\frac12M\lVert v_{\mathrm{boost}}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\Bigl(m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac12kR^{2}\Bigr)-2m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac12kR^{2},$$ the same value. Finally the scalar transfer of the potential is $U_{*}=U$ at corresponding data because $U$ depends only on $x_{1}-x_{2}=\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}$, so $\tilde E=\tilde K+U=\frac12kR^{2}+\frac12kR^{2}=kR^{2}$, and clause 5 gives $$\tilde E=E+\langle v_{\mathrm{boost}},P\rangle+\frac12M\lVert v_{\mathrm{boost}}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\Bigl(m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+kR^{2}\Bigr)-2m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}+m\lVert V\rVert_{2}^{2}=kR^{2},$$ again the same value.
